claim: Central nervous system (CNS) infections are a major cause of human morbidity and mortality worldwide.
source: Central nervous system (CNS) infections are a major cause of human morbidity and mortality worldwide.
evidence: This is a general statement about CNS infections that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: CNS infections can have lasting neurological dysfunction resulting from immune and pathogen induced pathology even in patients that survive.
source: Even patients that survive, CNS infections can have lasting neurological dysfunction resulting from immune and pathogen induced pathology.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the long-term consequences of CNS infections.

claim: A neurotropic virus (vesicular stomatitis virus) was introduced intranasally and entered the brain via olfactory sensory neurons in the murine model studied.
source: We studied a relevant murine model in which a neurotropic virus (vesicular stomatitis virus) was introduced intranasally and then entered the brain via olfactory sensory neurons – a route exploited by many pathogens in humans.
evidence: This describes the experimental model used in the study, which is supported by the methods and results presented.

claim: Small cerebral microbleeds were identified as an early form of pathology associated with viral entry into the brain using T2*-weighted high-resolution MRI.
source: Using T2*-weighted high-resolution MRI, we identified small cerebral microbleeds as an early form of pathology associated with viral entry into the brain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by MRI data presented in the results.

claim: Microbleeds occurred in the absence of peripheral immune cells.
source: Mechanistically, these microbleeds occurred in the absence of peripheral immune cells and were associated with infection of vascular endothelial cells.
evidence: This finding is supported by experiments using anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 antibodies to block immune cell infiltration, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Microbleeds were associated with infection of vascular endothelial cells.
source: Mechanistically, these microbleeds occurred in the absence of peripheral immune cells and were associated with infection of vascular endothelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data showing VSV in endothelial cells, as presented in Figure 4.

claim: Methods were developed to iron label and track individual virus specific CD8+ T cells by MRI.
source: We monitored the adaptive response to this infection by developing methods to iron label and track individual virus specific CD8+ T cells by MRI.
evidence: This is supported by the MPIO labeling methodology and MRI tracking data presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Transferred antiviral T cells were detected in the brain within a day of infection.
source: Transferred antiviral T cells were detected in the brain within a day of infection and were able to reduce cerebral microbleeds.
evidence: This is supported by MRI and histological data showing T cell presence at 24 hours post-infection, as shown in Figure 8.

claim: Transferred antiviral T cells were able to reduce cerebral microbleeds.
source: Transferred antiviral T cells were detected in the brain within a day of infection and were able to reduce cerebral microbleeds.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data comparing bleeding in mice with and without T cell transfer, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Viruses use multiple strategies to access the CNS.
source: Viruses use multiple strategies to access the CNS.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature on viral CNS entry mechanisms.

claim: Some viruses can infect the brain through the blood brain barrier (BBB) directly.
source: Some can infect the brain through the blood brain barrier (BBB) directly, whereas others enter the peripheral nervous system and use axonal transport along motor and olfactory neurons.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about viral entry routes into the CNS.

claim: Some viruses enter the peripheral nervous system and use axonal transport along motor and olfactory neurons.
source: Some can infect the brain through the blood brain barrier (BBB) directly, whereas others enter the peripheral nervous system and use axonal transport along motor and olfactory neurons.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about viral entry routes into the CNS.

claim: Infection of hematopoietic cells is used by some viruses to enter the CNS.
source: Infection of hematopoietic cells is also used to enter the CNS (McGavern and Kang, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Bleeding is one common pathology associated with viral infection.
source: One common pathology associated with viral infection is bleeding.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: Two major causes of virus-induced CNS bleeding are direct killing of infected cells and immune-mediated damage.
source: Two major causes of virus-induced CNS bleeding are direct killing of infected cells and immune-mediated damage (Ludlow et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Neural and glial inflammatory reactions play an important role in the defense against a viral infection.
source: Neural and glial inflammatory reactions play an important role in the defense against a viral infection (Chhatbar et al., 2018), as do innate and adaptive immune cells recruited from the periphery (Manglani and McGavern, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Innate and adaptive immune cells recruited from the periphery play an important role in defense against viral infection.
source: Neural and glial inflammatory reactions play an important role in the defense against a viral infection (Chhatbar et al., 2018), as do innate and adaptive immune cells recruited from the periphery (Manglani and McGavern, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Antiviral T cells recruited into the brain in response to infection can be both helpful and harmful.
source: Antiviral T cells recruited into the brain in response to infection can be both helpful and harmful (Klein and Hunter, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Antiviral memory T cells adoptively transferred into mice persistently infected from birth with LCMV can clear virus from the brain without causing immunopathology.
source: For example, studies have shown that antiviral memory T cells adoptively transferred into mice persistently infected from birth with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) can clear virus from the brain without causing immunopathology (Herz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pathogen-specific CD8 T cells can trigger fatal vascular breakdown during cerebral malaria.
source: However, pathogen-specific CD8 T cells can also trigger fatal vascular breakdown, which has been observed during cerebral malaria (Belnoue et al., 2002; Riggle et al., 2020; Swanson et al., 2016), viral meningitis (Kim et al., 2009), and SARS-CoV-2 infection (Schwabenland et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pathogen-specific CD8 T cells can trigger fatal vascular breakdown during viral meningitis.
source: However, pathogen-specific CD8 T cells can also trigger fatal vascular breakdown, which has been observed during cerebral malaria (Belnoue et al., 2002; Riggle et al., 2020; Swanson et al., 2016), viral meningitis (Kim et al., 2009), and SARS-CoV-2 infection (Schwabenland et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pathogen-specific CD8 T cells can trigger fatal vascular breakdown during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: However, pathogen-specific CD8 T cells can also trigger fatal vascular breakdown, which has been observed during cerebral malaria (Belnoue et al., 2002; Riggle et al., 2020; Swanson et al., 2016), viral meningitis (Kim et al., 2009), and SARS-CoV-2 infection (Schwabenland et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MRI has been very useful for the detection of pathological changes in the CNS during viral infection.
source: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been very useful for the detection of pathological changes in the CNS during viral infection (Lee et al., 2021; Poyiadji et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microbleeds can be detected sensitively as punctate hypointensity spots on T2*-weighted MRI.
source: Microbleeds can be detected sensitively as punctate hypointensity spots on T2*-weighted MRI (gradient-recalled echo or susceptibility-weighted imaging) (Griffin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and is a well-established principle in MRI.

claim: In post-mortem brain tissue from COVID patients, microbleeds were detected by T2*-weighted MRI, which guided the histology studies of cerebrovascular pathology and associated inflammation.
source: In post-mortem brain tissue from COVID patients, microbleeds were detected by T2*-weighted MRI, which guided the histology studies of cerebrovascular pathology and associated inflammation (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Large areas of bleeding were readily detected in the turbinates at day 4 post-infection.
source: Large areas of bleeding were readily detected in the turbinates at day 4 (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The amount of bleeding in the turbinates increased from day 4–11 post-infection.
source: The amount of bleeding, as indicated by hypointense areas (red arrows), increased from day 4–11.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Two major sites of bleeding were detected by MRI in the OB.
source: Two major sites of bleeding were also detected by MRI in the OB (Figure 1B–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claim: Bleeding was observed at the edge of the bulb, in the olfactory nerve layer (ONL) and glomerular layer (GL).
source: Bleeding was observed at the edge of the bulb, in the olfactory nerve layer (ONL) and glomerular layer (GL), and at the center of the bulb near the granule cell layer (GCL).
evidence: This is supported by MRI and histological data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bleeding was observed at the center of the bulb near the granule cell layer (GCL).
source: Bleeding was observed at the edge of the bulb, in the olfactory nerve layer (ONL) and glomerular layer (GL), and at the center of the bulb near the granule cell layer (GCL).
evidence: This is supported by MRI and histological data shown in Figure 1.

claim: As early as day 4, in-vivo MRI revealed microbleeds and vessel rupture starting in the ONL and GL of the OB.
source: As early as day 4, in-vivo MRI revealed microbleeds and vessel rupture starting in the ONL and GL of the OB (red arrows; Figure 1B and C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by in-vivo MRI data shown in Figures 1B and C.

claim: On day 6, punctate hypointensities near the center of the OB were detected by in-vivo MRI.
source: On day 6, punctate hypointensities near the center of the OB were also detected by in-vivo MRI (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by in-vivo MRI data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The number of microbleeds in the OB increased from day 4–11.
source: The number of microbleeds in the OB increased from day 4–11.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: VSV infected OB very efficiently and viral titers reached ~104 plaque-forming units (PFU) on day 1.
source: A previous study (Moseman et al., 2020) reported that VSV infected OB very efficiently and viral titers reached ~104 plaque-forming units (PFU) on day 1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Viral titer peaked on day 6 at ~105 PFU before being cleared on day 8.
source: Viral titer peaked on day 6, ~105 PFU, before being cleared on day 8.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and viral RNA measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Microbleeds largely co-localized with sites of VSV replication in the brain.
source: Thus, microbleeds largely co-localized with sites of VSV replication in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemical data showing VSV and microbleeds in the same locations, as shown in Figures 1G and H.

claim: Punctate hypointensities were detected from frontal brain to midbrain beginning at day 4.
source: Punctate hypointensities were detected from frontal brain to midbrain beginning at day 4.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In most of the infected mice, microbleeds were detected in the orbital frontal cortex area and somatomotor areas of the cortex around day 4.
source: In most of the infected mice, microbleeds were detected in the orbital frontal cortex area and somatomotor areas of the cortex around day 4.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 2.

claim: On day 6, microbleeds were detected in the caudoputamen (CP) and thalamus (TH).
source: On day 6, microbleeds were detected in the caudoputamen (CP) and thalamus (TH).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 2.

claim: From day 8–11, microbleeds were observed from midbrain to hindbrain.
source: From day 8–11, microbleeds were observed from midbrain to hindbrain.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Foci of bleeding were ~100-fold greater in the OB than the brain.
source: Foci of bleeding (defined as spots/mm3) were ~100-fold greater in the OB than the brain.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of MRI data comparing bleeding in the OB versus other brain regions.

claim: The size of mouse OB was assumed to be ~2% of the brain by volume.
source: For these calculations, the size of mouse OB was assumed to be ~2% of the brain by volume (McGann, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Significantly increased expression of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 were found in the OB on day 6 of infection.
source: Significantly increased expression of vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1) and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) were found in the OB on day 6 of infection.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 vessel surface coverage was around 50% near the ONL/GL/EPL region.
source: VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 vessel surface coverage was around 50% near the ONL/GL/EPL region (Figure 3A) and around 30% near the center of the OB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C) using anti-CD31 or anti-PECAM-1 to stain the entire vessel.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 vessel surface coverage was around 30% near the center of the OB.
source: VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 vessel surface coverage was around 50% near the ONL/GL/EPL region (Figure 3A) and around 30% near the center of the OB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C) using anti-CD31 or anti-PECAM-1 to stain the entire vessel.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upregulation of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 were found in many other locations in the midbrain and hindbrain on day 6, including the thalamus.
source: Upregulation of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 were also found in many other locations in the midbrain and hindbrain on day 6, e.g., thalamus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 blockade antibodies decreased CD45+ cells over 95% in the OB on day 6.
source: Anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 blockade antibodies decreased CD45+ cells over 95% in the OB on day 6. n=4 per group. * p<0.0001.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment with anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 blockade antibodies increased bleeding in the turbinates.
source: Treatment with anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 blockade antibodies increased bleeding in the turbinates.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Upon treatment with anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 blocking antibodies, MRI detected bleeding earlier in the glomerular layer (GL) of the OB.
source: In the glomerular layer (GL) (D) and the granule cell layer (GCL) of OB (E), MRI detected bleeding earlier upon treatment with the blockade antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Upon treatment with anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 blocking antibodies, MRI detected bleeding earlier in the granule cell layer (GCL) of the OB.
source: In the glomerular layer (GL) (D) and the granule cell layer (GCL) of OB (E), MRI detected bleeding earlier upon treatment with the blockade antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A large area of hemorrhage was detected in the thalamus of anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 treated mice on day 6.
source: Axial and (G) coronal view of MRI of the brain showed a large area of hemorrhage at the thalamus of anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 treated mouse on day 6.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figures 3F and G.

claim: The volume of bleeding in the turbinates increased from 2.1 ± 0.8 mm3 to 5.0 ± 1.0 mm3 on day 6 in anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 treated mice.
source: As quantified in Figure 3H, the volume of hypointensity in the turbinates increased from 2.1 ± 0.8 mm3 to 5.0 ± 1.0 mm3 on day 6 in anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 treated mice, and the number of bleeding spots increased in the brain by ~2-fold.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The number of bleeding spots increased in the brain by ~2-fold in anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 treated mice.
source: As quantified in Figure 3H, the volume of hypointensity in the turbinates increased from 2.1 ± 0.8 mm3 to 5.0 ± 1.0 mm3 on day 6 in anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 treated mice, and the number of bleeding spots increased in the brain by ~2-fold.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Blockade of immune infiltration elevated viral RNA in the OB by ~2–3-fold on day 6.
source: In addition, blockade of immune infiltration elevated viral RNA in the OB by ~2–3-fold on day 6 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: VSV induces hemorrhage in the brain without involvement of the peripheral immune system.
source: Thus, VSV induces hemorrhage in the brain without involvement of the peripheral immune system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that blocking peripheral immune cell infiltration did not prevent bleeding, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Inhibition of peripheral immune infiltration increased viral RNA, which was associated with more bleeding.
source: In fact, inhibition of peripheral immune infiltration increased viral RNA, which was associated with more bleeding.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figures 3H and 3I showing increased bleeding and viral RNA in mice treated with blocking antibodies.

claim: VSV was previously shown to enter the brain through olfactory sensory neurons via retrograde trans-neuronal transport.
source: VSV was previously shown to enter the brain through olfactory sensory neurons via retrograde trans-neuronal transport and spread in the CNS via both anterograde and retrograde transport (Beier et al., 2013; Cornish et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VSV spreads in the CNS via both anterograde and retrograde transport.
source: VSV was previously shown to enter the brain through olfactory sensory neurons via retrograde trans-neuronal transport and spread in the CNS via both anterograde and retrograde transport (Beier et al., 2013; Cornish et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most VSV-infected neurons in the brain are cleared noncytolytically.
source: Although VSV is highly cytopathic, most VSV-infected neurons in the brain are cleared noncytolytically (Moseman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VSV was detected in endothelial cells comprising cerebral blood vessels.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and B, we detected VSV in endothelial cells comprising cerebral blood vessels, which sometimes showed evidence of bleeding (Figure 4C and quantified in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: VSV-infected cerebral blood vessels sometimes showed evidence of bleeding.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and B, we detected VSV in endothelial cells comprising cerebral blood vessels, which sometimes showed evidence of bleeding (Figure 4C and quantified in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Infection of cerebrovascular endothelial cells by VSV may contribute to the mechanism responsible for bleeding.
source: These data suggest that infection of cerebrovascular endothelial cells by VSV may contribute to the mechanism responsible for bleeding.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of VSV in endothelial cells and associated bleeding.

claim: 5 × 10^5 virus-specific mTomato CD8+ OT-I T cells activated overnight with OVA257–264 peptide were transferred i.v. into VSV-OVA infected mice.
source: 5 × 105 virus-specific mTomato CD8+ OT-I T cells (purity shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1) activated overnight with ovalbumin (OVA)257–264 peptide were transferred i.v. into VSV-OVA infected mice at two time points.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: For early-stage transfer, OT-I cells were transferred on day 0–2, and MRI was performed on day 6.
source: For early-stage transfer, OT-I cells were transferred on day 0–2, and MRI was performed on day 6.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: For peak-stage transfer, OT-I cells were transferred on day 6 and mice were imaged on day 11.
source: For peak-stage transfer, OT-I cells were transferred on day 6 and mice were imaged on day 11 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Adoptive transfer of OT-I cells had a therapeutic benefit in both early- and peak-late-stage paradigms.
source: Adoptive transfer of OT-I cells had a therapeutic benefit in both early- and peak-late-stage paradigms (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data showing reduced bleeding in mice receiving T cell transfers, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: For peak-late-stage treatment, the volume of bleeding in the turbinates decreased from 12.2 ± 1.3 mm3 to 1.6 ± 1.1 mm3 on day 11.
source: For peak-late-stage treatment, in the turbinates (representative images shown in Figure 5A), the volume of bleeding decreased from 12.2 ± 1.3 mm3 to 1.6 ± 1.1 mm3 on day 11 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In the OB, the number of hypointensity spots decreased from 665 ± 127 to 114 ± 23 on day 11 after T cell transfer.
source: In the OB (Figure 5B), the number of hypointensity spots decreased from 665 ± 127–114 ± 23 on day 11 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In the brain, the number of hypointensity spots decreased from 329 ± 72 to 83 ± 19 on day 11 after T cell transfer.
source: In the brain (Figure 5D), the number of hypointensity spots decreased from 329 ± 72 to 83 ± 19 on day 11 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: T cell transfer reduced viral RNA in the OB for early stage transfer, with relative VSV to actin RNA decreasing from 0.95 ± 0.37 to 0.29 ± 0.07.
source: T cell transfer reduced microbleeds (Figure 5B and C) and also reduced viral RNA in the OB for early stage transfer. Relative VSV to actin RNA decreased from 0.95 ± 0.37 to 0.29 ± 0.07 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Without T cell transfer, there was a large amount of VSV and microbleeds, and a small number of CD8 T cells at the ONL, GL on day 6.
source: IHC confirmed that, without T cell transfer, there was a large amount of VSV and microbleeds, and a small number of CD8 T cells at the ONL, GL (Figure 6A), and center of the OB on day 6 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GL and OB center were major sites of virus invasion and replication.
source: Figure 6A and D also showed that GL and OB center were major sites of virus invasion and replication, which was consistent with Figure 1H.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figures 6A and D, consistent with earlier findings in Figure 1H.

claim: Upon transfer of OT-I cells, an increased number of CD8+ T cells, and a reduced amount of VSV and microbleeds was observed in the GL.
source: Upon transfer of OT-I cells, an increased number of CD8+ T cells, and a reduced amount of VSV and microbleeds was observed in the GL (Figure 6B) and OB center (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Upon transfer of OT-I cells, an increased number of CD8+ T cells, and a reduced amount of VSV and microbleeds was observed in the OB center.
source: Upon transfer of OT-I cells, an increased number of CD8+ T cells, and a reduced amount of VSV and microbleeds was observed in the GL (Figure 6B) and OB center (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Some microbleeds were still seen in mice receiving antiviral T cells, especially in regions with a high density of T cells.
source: Some microbleeds, however, were still seen in mice receiving antiviral T cells, especially in regions with a high density of T cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Administering a higher number of virus-specific CD8+ T cells (3 × 10^6 T cells) on day 6 was pathogenic as detected by MRI and IHC.
source: However, having too many antiviral T cells can also elevate cerebral bleeding. Administering a higher number of virus-specific CD8+ T cells (3 × 106 T cells, relative to the therapeutic lower dose 5 × 105) on day 6 was pathogenic as detected by MRI and IHC (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MRI and immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Antiviral CD8+ T cells at high doses can contribute to vessel damage while attempting to control virus.
source: This finding suggests that antiviral CD8+ T cells at high doses can contribute to vessel damage while attempting to control virus.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that high doses of T cells increased bleeding.

claim: The surface of streptavidin-MPIO particles was modified with cationic amine groups to increase the efficiency of uptake by T cells.
source: We therefore modified the surface of streptavidin-MPIO particles with cationic amine groups (Liu et al., 2012) to increase the efficiency of uptake by T cells.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to label T cells with MPIO particles.

claim: Anti-CD3 was conjugated to MPIO as an affinity ligand and to increase internalization of the particles by T cells.
source: In addition, anti-CD3 was conjugated to MPIO as an affinity ligand and to increase internalization of the particles by T cells.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to label T cells with MPIO particles.

claim: The yield of MPIO-labeled T cells was ~8.3%.
source: As shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, the yield of MPIO-labeled T cells was ~8.3% and the majority of MPIOs were localized inside the cells.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The majority of MPIOs were localized inside the cells.
source: As shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, the yield of MPIO-labeled T cells was ~8.3% and the majority of MPIOs were localized inside the cells.
evidence: This is supported by FACS and electron microscopy data shown in Figures 7B and 7E.

claim: 91% MPIOs were localized intracellularly.
source: 91% MPIOs were localized intracellularly (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: MPIO-labeled T cells showed MR sensitivity enabling single cell detection.
source: MPIO-labeled T cells showed MR sensitivity enabling single cell detection (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: There was no significant change in T cell migration function after MPIO labeling.
source: There was no significant change in these functions.
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: There was no significant change in IL-2 and IFN-gamma release after MPIO labeling.
source: There was no significant change in these functions.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine release assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E, F.

claim: At 15 hr post-infection, no hypointensities were detected in the OB by MRI.
source: At 15 hr post-infection, no hypointensities were detected in the OB by MRI (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: At 24 hr post-infection, the earliest hypointensity spots were detected near the GL.
source: At 24 hr post-infection, the earliest hypointensity spots were detected near the GL (Figure 8B) and the center, MCL/GCL areas of the bulb (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: At 24 hr post-infection, the earliest hypointensity spots were detected in the center, MCL/GCL areas of the bulb.
source: At 24 hr post-infection, the earliest hypointensity spots were detected near the GL (Figure 8B) and the center, MCL/GCL areas of the bulb (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: In the GL, CD8 T cell infiltration and bleeding co-localized and both occurred by 24 hr.
source: IHC showed that, in the GL, CD8 T cell infiltration and bleeding co-localized and both occurred by 24 hr (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The MRI hypointensity in the GL was caused by the combination of MRI contrast from MPIO-labeled T cells and microbleeds.
source: The MRI hypointensity in the GL was caused by the combination of MRI contrast from MPIO-labeled T cells and microbleeds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemical data showing both T cells and bleeding in the GL.

claim: 85% of MPIO-labeled T cells were in the region with microbleeds and 15% were in a region with no evidence of bleeding in the ONL/GL.
source: As quantified in Figure 8H, 85% of MPIO-labeled T cells were in the region with microbleeds and 15% were in a region with no evidence of bleeding in the ONL/GL.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Hypointensities in the MCL/GCL areas were due only to MPIO-labeled T cells, and no evidence for bleeding was detected.
source: Interestingly, hypointensities in the MCL/GCL areas were due only to MPIO-labeled T cells, and no evidence for bleeding was detected (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figures 8E-G.

claim: The appearance of hypointensity, caused by MPIO-labeled T cells was detected at 22 hr post-infection.
source: The appearance of hypointensity, caused by MPIO-labeled T cells was detected at 22 hr (Figure 8I, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse MRI data shown in Figure 8I and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: No migration tracks of T cells from ONL/GL to the center from MRI was detected.
source: No migration tracks of T cells from ONL/GL, where bleeding had already begun, to the center from MRI was detected.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse MRI data that did not show T cell movement between these regions.

claim: T cells at the center of the bulb likely extravasated from the local vasculature.
source: Thus, T cells at the center of the bulb likely extravasated from the local vasculature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of observed T cell migration from other regions.

claim: No evidence for T cell migration over a 2 hr time interval could be detected on the MRI distance scale.
source: No evidence for T cell migration over this 2 hr time interval could be detected on the MRI distance scale.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse MRI data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: On day 1, at the locations that CD8 T cells and microbleeds were detected, activation of vascular endothelium cells (as indicated by VCAM-1 and ICAM-1) and microglia (as indicated by CD68) were also detected by IHC.
source: On day 1, at the locations that CD8 T cells and microbleeds were detected, activation of vascular endothelium cells (as indicated by VCAM-1 and ICAM-1) and microglia (as indicated by CD68) were also detected by IHC (Figure 8J).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 8J.

claim: MRI of microbleeds and T cell tracking provides a noninvasive method for early detection of cerebrovascular inflammation.
source: Thus, MRI of microbleeds and T cell tracking provides a noninvasive method for early detection of cerebrovascular inflammation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing early detection of both microbleeds and T cells by MRI.

claim: The combination of MRI contrast from MPIO-labeled T cells and bleeds increased MRI sensitivity to areas where there was both microbleeds and T cell infiltration.
source: The combination of MRI contrast from MPIO-labeled T cells and bleeds increased MRI sensitivity to areas where there was both microbleeds and T cell infiltration (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that more hypointensity spots were detected when both T cells and bleeding were present.

claim: More hypointensity spots could be detected likely due to additive effects of bleeding and T cell detection.
source: More hypointensity spots could be detected likely due to additive effects of bleeding and T cell detection.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C, D.

claim: T2*-weighted MRI exhibits a high sensitivity to microbleeds due to paramagnetic properties of deoxy-hemoglobin from RBCs or its degradation product, hemosiderin.
source: T2*-weighted MRI exhibits a high sensitivity to microbleeds. This high sensitivity is due to paramagnetic properties of deoxy-hemoglobin from RBCs or its degradation product, hemosiderin (Haller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and reflects established knowledge about MRI physics.

claim: Paramagnetic and supermagnetic materials create a magnetic field gradient that is detected by T2*-weighted MRI and has an amplifying affect because the field gradients can extend at least 50 times greater than the actual size of the material.
source: Paramagnetic and supermagnetic materials create a magnetic field gradient that is detected by T2*-weighted MRI and has an amplifying affect because the field gradients can extend at least 50 times greater than the actual size of the material (Lauterbur et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and reflects established knowledge about MRI physics.

claim: Sensitivity down to ~1 pg iron per voxel can be achieved at high resolution MRI.
source: Sensitivity down ~1 pg iron per voxel can be achieved at high resolution (Shapiro et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: One RBC contains ~0.2 pg iron.
source: One RBC contains ~0.2 pg iron as calculated from Ozment and Turi, 2009.
evidence: This is based on a calculation from a cited reference.

claim: There is the potential to detect ~5–10 fully deoxygenated RBCs by MRI.
source: Thus, there is the potential to detect ~5–10 fully deoxygenated RBCs, which facilitates high sensitivity visualization of vessel bleeds where only a small amount of blood has entered the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the iron content per RBC and the sensitivity of MRI.

claim: MRI was shown to be more sensitive than CT to detect bleeding in human brain.
source: Thus, MRI was shown to be more sensitive than CT to detect bleeding in human brain.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent example of herpes simplex virus induced encephalitis.

claim: T2*-weighted MRI could detect bleeds in the brain within 2 days during the acute phases of herpes simplex virus induced encephalitis, whereas 1–2 weeks were required for CT-based detection.
source: For example, it was demonstrated in a study of herpes simplex virus induced encephalitis that T2*-weighted MRI could detect bleeds in the brain within 2 days during the acute phases of the disease, whereas 1–2 weeks were required for CT-based detection (Gupta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The presence of microbleeds in patients with stroke and traumatic brain injury is increasingly recognized as an indicator of worse outcome.
source: The presence of microbleeds in patients with stroke and traumatic brain injury is increasingly recognized as an indicator of worse outcome (Griffin et al., 2019; Haller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Iron deposition can initiate continued neuroinflammation and brain damage.
source: Iron deposition can initiate continued neuroinflammation and brain damage.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the effects of iron in the brain.

claim: MRI detected brain vessel damage and microbleeds in COVID patients was recently used to guide histological studies and uncover mechanisms of inflammation associated with SARS-CoV-2.
source: Indeed, MRI detected brain vessel damage and microbleeds in COVID patients was recently used to guide histological studies and uncover mechanisms of inflammation associated with SARS-CoV-2 (Lee et al., 2021; Riggle et al., 2020; Poyiadji et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Following i.n. inoculation, VSV replicated in the mouse lung, caused a transient viremia, and was found transiently in other organs, including liver and spleen.
source: Previous studies showed that following i.n. inoculation, VSV replicated in the mouse lung, caused a transient viremia, and was found transiently in other organs, including liver and spleen.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The virus was cleared from the periphery (lung, plasma, and liver) within 2–3 days post-infection.
source: The virus was cleared from the periphery (lung, plasma, and liver) within 2–3 days post-infection (Publicover et al., 2006; Ramsburg et al., 2005; Roberts et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Direct CNS infection, rather than peripheral pathology, causes brain microbleeds in this model.
source: Based on these results, we think that direct CNS infection, rather than peripheral pathology, causes brain microbleeds in this model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal pattern of viral infection and bleeding.

claim: VSV spike G-protein binds to low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDL-R) and enters cells via receptor-mediated endocytosis.
source: VSV spike G-protein binds to low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDL-R) and enters cells via receptor-mediated endocytosis (Nikolic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Endothelium of brain capillaries express LDL-R.
source: It was reported that endothelium of brain capillaries express LDL-R (Méresse et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A cell culture experiment showed that VSV-GFP infected and lysed endothelial cells.
source: In addition, a cell culture experiment showed that VSV-GFP infected and lysed endothelial cells (Patel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The peripheral immune response to VSV infection is important for the maintenance of vascular integrity and pathogen clearance.
source: The present study demonstrated that the peripheral immune response to VSV infection is important for the maintenance of vascular integrity and pathogen clearance, as blockade of CNS immune cell entry via administration of anti-LFA1/VLA4 antibodies increased brain bleeding and viral RNA (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3 showing increased bleeding and viral RNA when immune cell entry was blocked.

claim: Supplementing the immune response by adoptively transferring activated virus-specific CD8+ T cells at either early (day 0–2) or later (day 6) time points post-infection protected cerebral vessels.
source: Moreover, supplementing the immune response by adoptively transferring activated virus-specific CD8+ T cells at either early (day 0–2) or later (day 6) time points post-infection protected cerebral vessels.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5 showing reduced bleeding after T cell transfer.

claim: The transferred CD8+ T cells were not effective at completely blocking early viral entry from nasal olfactory sensory neurons into the OB.
source: The transferred CD8+ T cells were not effective at completely blocking early viral entry from nasal olfactory sensory neurons into the OB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some bleeding still occurred even with early T cell transfer.

claim: Adoptive transfer of MPIO-labeled virus-specific CD8+ T cells at the proper dose protected against brain bleeding at both early and late stages of infection.
source: Notably, at both early and late stages of infection, adoptive transfer of MPIO-labeled virus-specific CD8+ T cells at the proper dose protected against brain bleeding (Figures 1E and 2C versus Figure 8—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative MRI data comparing bleeding in mice with and without MPIO-labeled T cell transfer.

claim: MPIO-labeled CD8+ T cells retained their therapeutic functions.
source: Therefore, MPIO-labeled CD8+ T cells retained their therapeutic functions, indicating that the MPIO labeling did not have a negative effect on T cell functionality in-vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MPIO-labeled T cells were as effective as unlabeled T cells in reducing bleeding.

claim: VSV showed tropism for the neurons in the GL and GCL.
source: VSV showed tropism for the neurons in the GL and GCL and transferred virus-specific CD8+ T cells first arrived in these two layers between 15 and 24 hr post-infection.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data showing VSV in these layers.

claim: Transferred virus-specific CD8+ T cells first arrived in the GL and GCL between 15 and 24 hr post-infection.
source: VSV showed tropism for the neurons in the GL and GCL and transferred virus-specific CD8+ T cells first arrived in these two layers between 15 and 24 hr post-infection.
evidence: This is supported by MRI and immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 8.

claim: CD8+ T cells controlled neuronal virus in this model through engagements with cross-presenting microglia.
source: A previous study demonstrated that CD8+ T cells controlled neuronal virus in this model through engagements with cross-presenting microglia (Moseman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The GL and GCL of the bulb contain proliferating immature neurons in rodents.
source: These two layers of the bulb contain proliferating immature neurons in rodents (Batista-Brito et al., 2008; Lois and Alvarez-Buylla, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Immature neurons are generated by precursor cells in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and traffic through the rostral migratory stream (RMS) to different layers of the OB, primarily the GL and GCL, where they differentiate into neurons.
source: These immature neurons are generated by precursor cells in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and traffic through the rostral migratory stream (RMS) to different layers of the OB, primarily the GL and GCL, where they differentiate into neurons (Batista-Brito et al., 2008; Lois and Alvarez-Buylla, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many viruses have a tropism for immature neurons.
source: Many viruses have a tropism for immature neurons (Li et al., 2016), and the presence of immature neurons in these two layers may in part explain the tropism of VSV.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The presence of immature neurons in the GL and GCL may in part explain the tropism of VSV.
source: Many viruses have a tropism for immature neurons (Li et al., 2016), and the presence of immature neurons in these two layers may in part explain the tropism of VSV.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known tropism of viruses for immature neurons and the presence of such neurons in the GL and GCL.

claim: T cell velocities in the CNS have been clocked at ~10 µm/min.
source: Although T cell velocities in the CNS have been clocked at ~10 µm/min (Herz et al., 2015), their paths are often tortuous and influenced by antigen presenting cells displaying cognate peptide MHC as well as local chemokine gradients.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: T cell paths in the CNS are often tortuous and influenced by antigen presenting cells displaying cognate peptide MHC as well as local chemokine gradients.
source: Although T cell velocities in the CNS have been clocked at ~10 µm/min (Herz et al., 2015), their paths are often tortuous and influenced by antigen presenting cells displaying cognate peptide MHC as well as local chemokine gradients.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about T cell behavior in the CNS.

claim: VSV has the ability to cause vascular damage even at the early stages of infection.
source: In conclusion, our MRI guided studies have revealed that VSV has the ability to cause vascular damage even at the early stages of infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MRI and histological data showing early microbleeds.

claim: Vascular damage is worse if peripheral immune cell infiltration is blocked.
source: This damage is worse if peripheral immune cell infiltration is blocked and can be reduced by adoptively transferring antiviral T cells.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3 showing increased bleeding when immune cell infiltration was blocked.

claim: Vascular damage can be reduced by adoptively transferring antiviral T cells.
source: This damage is worse if peripheral immune cell infiltration is blocked and can be reduced by adoptively transferring antiviral T cells.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5 showing reduced bleeding after T cell transfer.

claim: Control of a CNS viral infection requires maintenance of a precise balance between reducing viral titer and preserving tissue integrity.
source: It is clear that control of a CNS viral infection requires maintenance of a precise balance between reducing viral titer and preserving tissue integrity, since transfer of too many T cells led to more extensive bleeding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that high doses of T cells increased bleeding.

claim: Transfer of too many T cells led to more extensive bleeding.
source: It is clear that control of a CNS viral infection requires maintenance of a precise balance between reducing viral titer and preserving tissue integrity, since transfer of too many T cells led to more extensive bleeding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MRI and histological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD8+ T cells can contribute to cerebrovascular pathology following Plasmodium berghei infection.
source: This is consistent with previous studies showing that CD8+ T cells can also contribute to cerebrovascular pathology following Plasmodium berghei infection (Swanson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MRI can be used to evaluate the extent of pathology after a CNS viral infection.
source: Identifying specific viral and immune mechanisms that result in cerebrovascular damage is a clinically relevant area of research, and our studies demonstrate that MRI can be used to evaluate the extent of pathology after a CNS viral infection as well as the efficacy of a therapeutic intervention like adoptive antiviral T cell transfer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MRI data presented throughout the study.

claim: MRI can be used to evaluate the efficacy of a therapeutic intervention like adoptive antiviral T cell transfer.
source: Identifying specific viral and immune mechanisms that result in cerebrovascular damage is a clinically relevant area of research, and our studies demonstrate that MRI can be used to evaluate the extent of pathology after a CNS viral infection as well as the efficacy of a therapeutic intervention like adoptive antiviral T cell transfer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MRI data showing reduced bleeding after T cell transfer.
